# Executive Summary & Workflow Overview

This R Markdown document contains the complete step-by-step workflow for **Part 1: Explore, Preprocess, and Quality-Control the Data**. 

Every code chunk includes explicit diagnostic output to report exactly what data points, features, or technical artifacts were adapted, filtered, or imputed during preprocessing.

---

# Step 0: Setup Working Directory & Load Packages

### Why this step is needed:
Setting the working directory ensures RStudio correctly locates your input CSV files. Installing and loading required libraries (`tidyverse`, `skimr`, `impute`, `limma`, `gridExtra`) provides tools for data wrangling, missingness audits, $k$-NN imputation, batch-effect correction, and PCA visualization.

### Lesson Reference:
*Lesson 2 – Chapter 2: Data Loading & Environment Setup*

```{r step0_setup}
# 0.1 Set local working directory
setwd("C:/Users/balde/Documents/UGent/Master/Master_1/Large scale analysis of biomedical data/PROJECT")

cat("==================================================================\n")
cat("STEP 0: ENVIRONMENT SETUP & PACKAGE AUDIT\n")
cat("==================================================================\n")
cat("Working directory set to:", getwd(), "\n\n")

# 0.2 Install & load required packages
required_packages <- c("tidyverse", "skimr", "impute", "limma", "gridExtra", "matrixStats")
new_packages <- required_packages[!(required_packages %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]

if(length(new_packages)) {
  cat("Installing missing packages:", paste(new_packages, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  if("impute" %in% new_packages || "limma" %in% new_packages) {
    if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
    if("impute" %in% new_packages) BiocManager::install("impute")
    if("limma" %in% new_packages) BiocManager::install("limma")
    new_packages <- setdiff(new_packages, c("impute", "limma"))
  }
  if(length(new_packages)) install.packages(new_packages)
}

library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
library(impute)  # Bioconductor package for k-NN imputation
library(limma)   # Bioconductor package for batch effect removal
library(gridExtra)

cat("All required R packages successfully loaded!\n")
```

---

# Step 1: Dataset Exploration & Variable Auditing

### Why this step is needed:
Before modifying data, we must inspect dimensions, sample IDs, and variable types. Variables are categorized into Nominal, Ordinal, Discrete Numeric, and Continuous Numeric types to ensure appropriate statistical handling.

### Lesson Reference:
*Lesson 2 – Step 1 & 1.2: Data Exploration: Describe Your Data*

```{r step1_exploration}
cat("==================================================================\n")
cat("STEP 1: DATA EXPLORATION & DIMENSION AUDIT\n")
cat("==================================================================\n")

# 1.1 Load raw CSV files
protein_annot <- read_csv("protein_annotation.csv")
sample_meta  <- read_csv("sample_metadata.csv")
npx_raw      <- read_csv("proteins_npx_raw.csv")

# 1.2 Report initial dimensions
cat("--- DATASET DIMENSIONS ---\n")
cat("1. Raw NPX Matrix    :", nrow(npx_raw), "sample rows x", ncol(npx_raw) - 1, "protein features\n")
cat("2. Sample Metadata   :", nrow(sample_meta), "sample rows x", ncol(sample_meta), "clinical columns\n")
cat("3. Protein Annotation:", nrow(protein_annot), "annotated protein assays\n\n")

# 1.3 Audit Variable Types in Metadata
cat("--- VARIABLE TYPE BREAKDOWN (Sample Metadata) ---\n")
cat("• Nominal Categorical : sample_kit_id, subject.subjectGuid, subject.biologicalSex, cmv_status, olink_plate_id, olink_batch_id\n")
cat("• Ordinal Categorical : subject.ageGroup (e.g. Young Adult, Older Adult), sample.visitName\n")
cat("• Discrete Numeric    : n_missing_npx, subject.birthYear, sample.drawYear\n")
cat("• Continuous Numeric  : Protein NPX log2 values, ageAtDraw, am.bmi, chem.creatinine, bc.wbc, infl.hs_crp\n\n")

# Print summary of metadata key variables
skim(sample_meta %>% select(subject.biologicalSex, subject.ageGroup, cmv_status, olink_plate_id, am.bmi))

# 1.4 Factor Conversion & Baseline Leveling (Preparing for Part 2 Regression Models)
cat("\n--- 1.4 METADATA FACTOR CONVERSION & BASELINE LEVELING ---\n")
sample_meta <- sample_meta %>%
  mutate(
    subject.ageGroup      = factor(subject.ageGroup),
    subject.ageGroup      = relevel(subject.ageGroup, ref = "Young Adult"),
    cmv_status            = factor(cmv_status),
    cmv_status            = relevel(cmv_status, ref = "Negative"),
    subject.biologicalSex = factor(subject.biologicalSex),
    subject.biologicalSex = relevel(subject.biologicalSex, ref = "Female"),
    olink_plate_id        = factor(olink_plate_id)
  )

cat("✔ Metadata Factors successfully converted & reference baselines set:\n")
cat("  • subject.ageGroup      : Reference level -> '", levels(sample_meta$subject.ageGroup)[1], "'\n", sep="")
cat("  • cmv_status            : Reference level -> '", levels(sample_meta$cmv_status)[1], "'\n", sep="")
cat("  • subject.biologicalSex : Reference level -> '", levels(sample_meta$subject.biologicalSex)[1], "'\n", sep="")
cat("  • olink_plate_id        : Total plate factor levels -> ", length(levels(sample_meta$olink_plate_id)), "\n\n")
```

---

# Step 2: Quality Control, Filtering & Imputation

### Why this step is needed:
1. **Duplicate Assay Filtering**: Duplicate gene symbol aliases mapping to identical Olink assay IDs create artificial redundancy and column errors (18 entries removed).
2. **Limit of Detection (LOD) & Missingness Thresholding (>20% NA / >50% LOD)**: 
   - **Limit of Detection (`pct_below_lod > 50%`)**: Proteins where >50% of sample values fall below the Limit of Detection (LOD) represent non-quantifiable background noise. Filtering these ~151 proteins prevents heavy artificial noise imputation, removes non-informative noise, and reduces the multiple-testing penalty in downstream statistical testing (Part 2 & 3).
   - **Missingness Thresholding (`pct_missing > 20%`)**: Any remaining proteins exceeding 20% explicit $NA$ values are removed.
3. **$k$-NN Imputation**: Setting missing NPX values to 0 distorts relative $\log_2$ scales ($2^0 = 1$). $k$-Nearest Neighbors imputation fills isolated missing values (<20% $NA$) using biological co-expression patterns.

### Lesson Reference:
*Lesson 2 – Step 2.1 & 2.2: Missing Values, Imputation & Filtering*

```{r step2_qc_filtering}
cat("==================================================================\n")
cat("STEP 2: QC FILTERING & IMPUTATION ADAPTATION OUTPUT\n")
cat("==================================================================\n")

# 2.1 Identify and remove duplicate Olink assay IDs
dup_rows <- protein_annot %>% filter(duplicate_olink_id == TRUE)
dup_proteins <- dup_rows %>% pull(protein)

cat("--- 2.1 DUPLICATE ASSAYS IDENTIFIED & REMOVED ---\n")
cat("Number of duplicate protein aliases found:", length(dup_proteins), "\n")
cat("Duplicate protein symbols removed:\n")
print(dup_rows %>% select(protein, olink_id, same_assay_as))
cat("\n")

# 2.2 Calculate Missingness & LOD Rates per Protein
npx_mat_raw <- npx_raw %>% column_to_rownames("sample_kit_id")
total_initial_cells <- nrow(npx_mat_raw) * ncol(npx_mat_raw)
total_initial_nas   <- sum(is.na(npx_mat_raw))

# Identify proteins with >50% measurements below LOD (~151 proteins)
high_lod_proteins <- protein_annot %>% 
  filter(pct_below_lod > 50) %>% 
  pull(protein)

# Identify proteins with >20% explicit NAs
protein_missingness <- colMeans(is.na(npx_mat_raw)) * 100
high_missing_proteins <- names(protein_missingness[protein_missingness > 20])

# Combine all exclusion targets
all_removed_proteins <- unique(c(dup_proteins, high_lod_proteins, high_missing_proteins))
all_removed_proteins <- intersect(all_removed_proteins, colnames(npx_mat_raw))

cat("--- 2.2 MISSINGNESS & LOD AUDIT & EXCLUSION ---\n")
cat("Total matrix cells                :", total_initial_cells, "\n")
cat("Total initial NA values           :", total_initial_nas, "(", round(total_initial_nas / total_initial_cells * 100, 3), "%)\n")
cat("Proteins exceeding 50% below LOD  :", length(high_lod_proteins), "proteins filtered out\n")
cat("Proteins exceeding 20% NAs        :", length(high_missing_proteins), "proteins filtered out\n")
cat("Total unique proteins removed     :", length(all_removed_proteins), "proteins\n\n")

# Apply feature filtering
valid_proteins <- setdiff(colnames(npx_mat_raw), all_removed_proteins)
npx_filtered <- npx_mat_raw[, valid_proteins]

cat("--- FEATURE SELECTION SUMMARY ---\n")
cat("Initial protein features          :", ncol(npx_mat_raw), "\n")
cat("Total Removed (LOD + Dups + NAs)  :", length(all_removed_proteins), "\n")
cat("Final Retained Proteins           :", ncol(npx_filtered), "\n\n")

# Plot Missingness & LOD Distributions
df_lod <- protein_annot %>% filter(protein %in% colnames(npx_mat_raw))
p_lod <- ggplot(df_lod, aes(x = pct_below_lod)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "darkred", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, color = "yellow", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Protein % Below LOD",
       x = "Percentage Below LOD (%)", y = "Protein Count",
       caption = "Yellow line indicates 50% LOD exclusion threshold") +
  theme_minimal()
print(p_lod)

# 2.3 Apply k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) Imputation
nas_before_knn <- sum(is.na(npx_filtered))
cat("--- 2.3 k-NN IMPUTATION ADAPTATION ---\n")
cat("Isolated NAs remaining in filtered matrix before k-NN:", nas_before_knn, "\n")

npx_transposed <- t(as.matrix(npx_filtered))
knn_result <- impute.knn(npx_transposed, k = 10, rowmax = 0.5, colmax = 0.8)
npx_imputed <- t(knn_result$data) # Transpose back to Samples x Proteins

nas_after_knn <- sum(is.na(npx_imputed))
cat("Isolated NAs remaining after k-NN imputation       :", nas_after_knn, "\n")
cat("Status: Matrix is now 100% complete and ready for scaling!\n\n")
```

---

# Step 3: Data Transformation & Standardization ($Z$-Score Scaling)

### Why this step is needed:
Olink NPX values are already $\log_2$-transformed by default. To prevent highly abundant proteins from dominating PCA variance or machine learning weights, features are standardized ($Z$-score scaling: mean $= 0$, standard deviation $= 1$).

### Lesson Reference:
*Lesson 2 – Step 2.4 (Log-Transformation) & Step 2.5 (Standardization)*

```{r step3_standardization}
cat("==================================================================\n")
cat("STEP 3: STANDARDIZATION & SCALING ADAPTATION OUTPUT\n")
cat("==================================================================\n")

# 3.1 Verify log2 scale (No additional log-transform required)
cat("Log-Transform Check: NPX data is already on a log2 scale.\n")

# 3.2 Z-Score Standardization
npx_scaled <- scale(npx_imputed)

# 3.3 Print summary verification of scaled matrix
col_means <- mean(colMeans(npx_scaled))
col_sds   <- mean(apply(npx_scaled, 2, sd))

cat("--- Z-SCORE SCALING VERIFICATION ---\n")
cat("Overall Matrix Mean (Target = 0) :", round(col_means, 6), "\n")
cat("Overall Matrix SD   (Target = 1) :", round(col_sds, 6), "\n")
cat("All", ncol(npx_scaled), "proteins successfully centered and scaled.\n\n")
```

---

# Step 4: Quality Control & PCA Batch Correction

### Why this step is needed:
PCA evaluates sample clustering. In the raw data, samples cluster strongly by laboratory plate (`olink_plate_id`), indicating that technical batch effects dominate global variance. We apply `limma::removeBatchEffect()` while preserving the biological design (`subject.ageGroup`) to remove plate artifacts and unmask true biological signals.

### Lesson Reference:
*Lesson 2 – Step 3.2.3 (PCA & Clustering) & Step 4 (Batch Effects)*

```{r step4_pca_batch_correction, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
cat("==================================================================\n")
cat("STEP 4: PCA & BATCH EFFECT REMOVAL DIAGNOSTICS\n")
cat("==================================================================\n")

# 4.1 Uncorrected PCA
pca_raw <- prcomp(npx_scaled, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
var_raw <- (pca_raw$sdev^2) / sum(pca_raw$sdev^2) * 100

cat("--- RAW PCA VARIANCE EXPLAINED ---\n")
cat("PC1:", round(var_raw[1], 2), "% | PC2:", round(var_raw[2], 2), "% | Combined Top 2 PCs:", round(var_raw[1] + var_raw[2], 2), "%\n\n")

# 4.2 Apply Batch Correction using limma
cat("--- APPLYING LIMMA BATCH CORRECTION ---\n")
cat("Technical Batch Factor Removed : olink_plate_id (", length(unique(sample_meta$olink_plate_id)), "unique plates)\n")
cat("Biological Design Preserved    : subject.ageGroup\n")

npx_transposed_scaled <- t(npx_scaled)
batch_plate <- sample_meta$olink_plate_id
design_bio  <- model.matrix(~ subject.ageGroup, data = sample_meta)

npx_corrected_transposed <- removeBatchEffect(
  x = npx_transposed_scaled,
  batch = batch_plate,
  design = design_bio
)

npx_batch_corrected <- t(npx_corrected_transposed)

# 4.3 Corrected PCA
pca_corr <- prcomp(npx_batch_corrected, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
var_corr <- (pca_corr$sdev^2) / sum(pca_corr$sdev^2) * 100

cat("--- BATCH-CORRECTED PCA VARIANCE EXPLAINED ---\n")
cat("PC1:", round(var_corr[1], 2), "% | PC2:", round(var_corr[2], 2), "% | Combined Top 2 PCs:", round(var_corr[1] + var_corr[2], 2), "%\n\n")

# 4.4 Prepare Visualization Comparisons
df_pca_raw  <- as.data.frame(pca_raw$x[, 1:2]) %>% 
  rownames_to_column("sample_kit_id") %>% 
  inner_join(sample_meta, by = "sample_kit_id")

df_pca_corr <- as.data.frame(pca_corr$x[, 1:2]) %>% 
  rownames_to_column("sample_kit_id") %>% 
  inner_join(sample_meta, by = "sample_kit_id")

# Raw Plate Effect Plot
p1 <- ggplot(df_pca_raw, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = olink_plate_id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  labs(title = "Raw PCA: Technical Plate Batches",
       subtitle = "Strong separation by olink_plate_id",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", round(var_raw[1], 1), "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", round(var_raw[2], 1), "%)")) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")

# Corrected Plate Effect Plot
p2 <- ggplot(df_pca_corr, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = olink_plate_id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  labs(title = "Batch-Corrected PCA: Plate Effect Removed",
       subtitle = "Plates homogenously intermixed",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", round(var_corr[1], 1), "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", round(var_corr[2], 1), "%)")) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")

# Corrected Biological Signal Plot (Age Group)
p3 <- ggplot(df_pca_corr, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = `subject.ageGroup`)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 1.8) +
  labs(title = "Corrected PCA: Biological Signal",
       subtitle = "Evaluated by Age Group",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", round(var_corr[1], 1), "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", round(var_corr[2], 1), "%)")) +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3)
```

---

# Step 5: Export Final Cleaned & Batch-Corrected Dataset

### Why this step is needed:
Exporting the processed dataset to `.rds` and `.csv` formats creates a reproducible checkpoint for downstream multivariable linear regression (Parts 2 & 3) and machine learning classification (Part 4).

```{r step5_export}
cat("==================================================================\n")
cat("STEP 5: DATASET EXPORT & FINAL SUMMARY VERIFICATION\n")
cat("==================================================================\n")

# Save cleaned objects (both protein matrix and factor-leveled metadata)
saveRDS(npx_batch_corrected, "preprocessed_proteins_npx_batch_corrected.rds")
write.csv(as.data.frame(npx_batch_corrected), "preprocessed_proteins_npx_batch_corrected.csv")

saveRDS(sample_meta, "sample_metadata_processed.rds")
write.csv(sample_meta, "sample_metadata_processed.csv")

cat("--- PREPROCESSING FINAL CHECKLIST ---\n")
cat("✔ Final Samples Count       : ", nrow(npx_batch_corrected), "\n")
cat("✔ Final Retained Proteins   : ", ncol(npx_batch_corrected), "\n")
cat("✔ Remaining Missing Values  : ", sum(is.na(npx_batch_corrected)), "\n")
cat("✔ Z-Score Scaling Complete  :  Mean = 0, SD = 1\n")
cat("✔ Batch Correction Applied  :  olink_plate_id effect removed via limma\n")
cat("✔ Output Files Saved        : 'preprocessed_proteins_npx_batch_corrected.rds', 'sample_metadata_processed.rds' & CSVs\n")
cat("==================================================================\n")
cat("PART 1 PREPROCESSING COMPLETE AND READY FOR PART 2 MODELING!\n")
cat("==================================================================\n")
```
